summary: A 1975 extension to FTP for transferring files in page mode between TENEX systems. It also discusses how reliable such file transfers are. It updates RFC 354.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 683 describes an experimental FTP type for transferring TENEX files as numbered chunks. The chunks preserve the file's page layout and attributes, and the receiver checks their order and contents.

questions: how did tenex transfer paged files over ftp
what is in an xtp chunk header
subtitle: An experimental FTP type for transferring TENEX files page by page.

tldr.problem: TENEX files can contain missing pages and file attributes that ordinary FTP transfer did not preserve. The author also wanted checksums and sequence numbers for network transfers.
tldr.mechanism: The experimental XTP type sends chunks with a checksum, sequence number, data length, page number, access bits and a type code, followed by the data.
tldr.outcome: RFC 683 extends the OLD FTP protocol and updates RFC 354. The author calls the design incorrect and expects a proper approach to be negotiated in the NEW protocol, RFC 542.

facts.label: Chunk types
facts.value: 0 for a data page; -3 for an FDB

today: RFC 683 updates RFC 354; the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and names no later RFC that updates or replaces it. The RFC itself calls XTP an experimental implementation and points to RFC 542 for a possible correct design.

sections.title: Why FTP Needed an Extension
sections.content:
RFC 683 extends the OLD FTP protocol so TENEX paged files can be transferred over the network. The author also wanted a transfer mode with checksums and block sequence numbers, and suggested that data compression could be useful.

He says a correct design would likely use new MODE and STRUcture settings. Instead, he implemented the features as one new TYPE to reduce the changes needed in FTP user and server programs, while acknowledging that the choice may be incorrect.
sections.plainLanguage: TENEX files have a page-based layout that FTP could not transfer as needed. The author chose one new FTP setting as a smaller implementation change, but says it may not be the right design.

sections.title: The TENEX File Layout
sections.content:
A TENEX file has a pathname, a page table, pages and attributes stored in a File Descriptor Block (FDB). The page table can contain up to 2**18 entries. An entry may be empty or point to a page, and each page can have its own access bits.

Each page contains 512 words of 36 bits. Pages do not have to be adjacent in the page table, so a file can contain holes. The end-of-file pointer is also not required to point at the last datum. The RFC says these cases occur in NLS data files.
sections.plainLanguage: A TENEX file records which page positions contain data and which are empty. It also stores file details separately, so a transfer must carry both the pages and those details.

sections.title: The XTP Chunk Format
sections.content:
The new type is XTP: X marks it as experimental, T identifies TENEX and P means paged. It is implemented only for STRU F, BYTE 36 and MODE S. Each chunk begins with a word stating how many header words follow; that count is currently 6. The header then comes before the data words.

The six header words contain a checksum, a sequence number, the number of data words, the page number, access bits and a chunk type. Empty page positions are not sent, and a hole is not the same as a page of zeroes. The current chunk types are 0 for a data page and -3 for an FDB. The receiver reports an error for a bad checksum, wrong sequence, unreasonable data length or a file that does not end immediately after an FDB chunk.
sections.plainLanguage: Each chunk carries information that lets the receiver check its contents, order and place in the file. Empty page positions are skipped, while the file's descriptor block must come last.

sections.title: Implementation and Intended Scope
sections.content:
The author reports that the FTP server and user were operating on all BBN systems and at some other sites. He expects checksumming and sequencing to be addressed in the NEW FTP protocol, and describes RFC 683 as an implementation note that lets users connect to TENEX sites installing the extension.

The RFC updates RFC 354 and points to RFC 542 as the place where a correct design might be negotiated. The author also asks readers to comment on whether FTP's MODE, TYPE and STRUcture settings adequately describe data transfers.
sections.plainLanguage: This document describes a working experimental extension, not a final design. The author expects a later FTP protocol to address the broader transfer features.
